issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
covered_actors: AI system stakeholders (organizations and teams that commission, fund, procure, develop, or deploy AI systems; business, design, development, internal risk management, and compliance teams)
Operators and evaluators (academic, public, and private sector researchers; professional evaluators and auditors; system operators; expert end users)
External stakeholders (trade groups, standards developing organizations, advocacy groups, civil society organizations)
Small to medium-sized organizations and large organizations across all sectors

evidence.quote: This voluntary framework provides a flexible, 30 structured, and measurable process to address AI risks throughout the AI lifecycle, offering 31 guidance for the development and use of trustworthy and responsible AI.

Potential harms of the AI system are elucidated along technical and socio-technical characteristics and aligned with guiding principles. Likelihood of each harm is understood based on expected use, past uses of AI systems in similar contexts, public incident reports or other data.

Operators and evaluators provide monitoring and formal/informal test, evaluation, validation, 15 and verification (TEVV) of system performance, relative to both technical and socio-technical 16 requirements.

Accuracy, reliability, robustness, resilience (or ML security), explainability and interpretability, privacy, safety, bias, and other system performance or assurance criteria are measured, qualitatively or quantitatively.

Data generated from experiments that are 26 designed to evaluate system performance also fall into this category and might include tests of 27 causal hypotheses and assessments of robustness to adversarial attack.

Transparency reflects the extent to which information is available to a 24 user when interacting with an AI system. Its scope spans from design decisions and training data 25 to model training, the structure of the model, its intended use case, how and when deployment 26 decisions were made and by whom, etc.

Priority actions to maximize benefits and minimize harm are planned, prepared, implemented, and communicated to internal and external stakeholders as appropriate (or required) and to the extent practicable.
The risk management process and its outcomes are documented and traceable through transparent mechanisms, as appropriate and to the extent practicable.
Intended purpose, setting in which the AI system will be deployed, the specific set of users along with their expectations, and impacts of system use are understood and documented as appropriate.

Ideally, this evaluation should be conducted by an independent third party or by experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system, and who consults experts, stakeholders, and impacted communities.
Other common ML security concerns relate to the 16 exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints.
evidence.source_section: Part 1: Motivation - 5.1.4 Resilience or ML Security

evidence.quote: Mechanisms are in place and maintained to supersede, disengage, or deactivate existing applications of AI that demonstrate performance or outcomes that are inconsistent with their intended use.
Plans related to post deployment monitoring of the systems are implemented, including mechanisms for user feedback, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, and change management.
Considerations related to data collection and selection are identified. (e.g., availability, representativeness, suitability).
Policies and procedures include guidelines for ensuring supply chain and partner involvement and expectations regarding the value and trustworthiness of third-party data or AI systems.
The AI RMF is intended for voluntary use in addressing risks in the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems.
It is important to note that the AI RMF is neither a checklist nor should be used in any way to certify an AI system.

implementation_notes: Superseded consultation draft of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework published March 17, 2022 (public comment deadline April 29, 2022; later superseded by the August 18, 2022 Second Draft and January 26, 2023 AI RMF 1.0). Organizes trustworthiness into a three-class taxonomy (technical characteristics, socio-technical characteristics, guiding principles) and introduces the four Core functions (Map, Measure, Manage, Govern). Explicitly voluntary, outcome-focused, non-prescriptive, law- and regulation-agnostic, and defers Profiles, Effectiveness, and the companion Practice Guide to subsequent drafts.
